text:
Where in the world can you get a professional-level, in-depth tour of an important monument or museum for free?
Seoul, that’s where. And the Youth Exchanging Culture Communicators’ Organization (YECCO) is who.
I recently joined them for a “Histour” of Gyeongbok Palace. The name signals the tour's focus on historical interpretation and information. The day was crisp, but bright and beautiful — perfect for exploring the nooks and crannies of the sprawling complex.
My guides were YECCO President Kang Min-su and two very capable assistants, Kang Seo-hyun and Jeon Ju-hyeon. YECCO is a group of dynamic university students making a significant contribution to the city and nation by introducing Korea to the world.
Knowing of my lifelong engagement with Korea, one of the first questions my guides asked me was, “How many times have you visited Gyeongbok Palace?”
“Countless,” I answered. My first visit was some 50 years ago. That marks me as a most unusual guest for a guided tour of the place and was perhaps a bit intimidating to my guides. However, I was in exploratory mode and wanted to learn more about YECCO and its members. I tried to put the team at ease and asked them to conduct the tour as they would for any guest.
The level of detail and the insight into some of the smaller details of the huge palace complex, many of which I hadn't known, deeply impressed me. Min-su was a great teacher. He insisted that I repeat, after him, the names of each of the large buildings we visited — in the Korean pronunciation of the "hanja" (traditional characters) signs prominently placed over each entrance.
Min-su, a 24-year-old who currently attends Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, led the day's tour. He is a passionate youth, majoring in language and diplomacy. His assistants are equally impressive. Seo-hyun, 23, majors in nursing at Seoul National University and Ju-hyeon, 23, is studying history at Sungshin Women’s University.
Founded in 2016, the organization is an independent, self-sustaining university student organization. YECCO is not the typical university club. They have officially registered nonprofit status. Active members who have served for at least two years are eligible to join the alum association. Alum members may occasionally participate in the organization's activities but are not required to take an active role.
In 2018, Royal Asiatic Society (RAS) Korea and YECCO signed a memorandum of understanding to foster a cooperative relationship between the two organizations. Members are welcome at regular RAS Korea lectures and often attend other society programs.
New members of YECCO are recruited each spring as the new school year begins. There is no limit on major, but members need a working knowledge of Korean cultural heritage to achieve the organization's mission.
Under the banner of “Korea’s heritage meets the world through youth,” YECCO has three main mission objectives. First, connect traditional and modern culture by increasing the number of young people who appreciate Korea's history and culture. Second, through its systematic education program, it develops global cultural communicators through international exchange programs and other projects that promote Korea’s history and culture. YECCO's success hinges on its third objective, building a youth-led volunteer community.
YECCO works with several multinational organizations to design programs and host events. This impressive list of connections includes Academic Programs International and the Council on International Education Exchange. They also engage with the Global Overseas Adoptees Association and run programs with the annual MoMo Camp. The camp is organized by Modu Moida, which helps second-generation and multigenerational overseas Koreans connect with their heritage.
A foundational principle of YECCO’s goals is to show the world that Korean cultural heritage is deeper and richer than K-dramas, K-cosmetics and K-pop, no matter how important those elements may be.
The organization's most public engagement is YECCO’s connection with Seoul’s Jongno-gu Volunteer Center, which provides identification badges for YECCO’s tour guide program and helps manage volunteer service records.
Each weekend throughout the year, YECCO members descend on Gyeongbok Palace to offer free “Histours” to foreign guests. Guides do not accept tips from guests, in line with national regulations and the palace management organization. Guests are asked to pay a nominal admission fee to enter the palace grounds.
The goal of the guide program is to connect, and YECCO approaches the task with the highest professional standards. I can say with confidence that YECCO volunteers offer a fantastic tour experience.
Before becoming qualified tour guides, all YECCO members must complete a designated training curriculum. The curriculum is researched and developed by the organization, then reviewed by relevant research institutions and university professors before being used for member training.
From March to August, members attend monthly lectures covering assigned topics and write their own tour scenarios based on the material covered each month. Mentors work with members one-on-one to review their scenarios, provide feedback and help refine their content.
Upon completing the curriculum in August, members compile their work into a final tour scenario. They must then pass the assessments based on this scenario: an on-site rehearsal, an oral examination and a written examination.
English is the lingua franca of the tours, but several YECCO members are multilingual. Efforts are underway to expand the tours to other locations in Seoul.
Members of the organization are required to conduct at least one tour each month. They do this in teams of three or four, so the engagement with tourists is a small-group, relational experience.
YECCO currently has about 100 members. Over the past couple of years, more than 300 volunteer guides have hosted over 2,000 guests from more than 50 countries. The total number going back to the start is estimated to be around 1,000 volunteers. Those are impressive statistics for full-time university students. The numbers are similar for exchange programs and various collaborations.
Members of YECCO also have several common interest groups to foster relationships among themselves. These include YECCO Class, where members host gatherings to explore history and culture, including field trips to Korea's historic and cultural destinations. YECCO Community brings members together through shared hobbies and casual meetups, such as sports, photography and food. The organization also supports several active columnists who create content online.
Regular attendance at monthly meetings is required. Business matters are attended to, educational elements are included and there is often a guest speaker. I was honored to be the special guest lecturer last month. I found it exhilarating to talk with a group of some of Korea’s finest youth. Their questions and comments were thoughtful and showed a deep worldview that today's society needs.
Even if you’ve been to Gyeongbok Palace before, why not give a YECCO-led tour a try? Visit yecco.or.kr for more information and to book a tour. I can’t think of any better way to spend a weekend in Seoul!
Rev. Steven L. Shields, FRAS, has lived in Korea for many years, beginning in the 1970s. A fellow of the Royal Asiatic Society of Great Britain and Ireland, he is also a life member of Royal Asiatic Society Korea, where he served as director, vice president and president. He was a copy editor of The Korea Times in 1977.
